Eiffel proved how far static rigor could reach—and where its edges sharpened.

Now our story leaps to its boldest extreme yet. Back in California, two researchers asked an audacious question: *what if object-oriented programming had no classes at all?*

questions.prompt: How does the 'catcall' pitfall of covariant arguments connect directly back to Section 5's subcontracting rules?
choices: Narrowing an argument type weakens the precondition, allowing subclasses to accept broader unexpected inputs.
Narrowing an argument type removes the class invariant so stored balances can turn negative.
Narrowing an argument type strengthens the postcondition, forcing callers to expect narrower return outputs.
Narrowing an argument type tightens the precondition, rejecting valid inputs the parent contract promised.
questions.explanation: Just like tightening a 'require' clause, narrowing an argument from 'Food' to 'Grass' refuses valid inputs the parent contract promised to accept.

questions.prompt: Which variance rule did later statically typed languages adopt after learning from Eiffel's covariant-argument trap?
choices: Subclasses may safely narrow input argument types, while return types must grow broader.
Subclasses may safely narrow return types, while narrowing input argument types breaks substitution.
Subclasses must keep both return and input types frozen and ban all subclass substitution.
Subclasses should skip compile-time variance rules and route mismatched calls to silent zero returns.
questions.explanation: Returning a more specific subtype (covariant output) always satisfies callers expecting the broader parent type, whereas narrowing inputs breaks safe substitution.

sections.title: 7. Self's Radical Minimalism: Prototypes, Cloning & Uniform Slots
sections.summary: Introduces David Ungar and Randall Smith's Self—sparked at Xerox PARC and built at Stanford and Sun Labs—which asked whether object orientation needed classes at all. Explains from first principles how Self replaced abstract class blueprints with concrete prototype exemplars copied by cloning, collapsed data fields and methods into uniform slots accessed identically via messages, and shared behavior dynamically through delegating parent slots inside a tactile, live graphical world.

chunks.title: What If Classes Were the Problem?
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1986, two researchers at Xerox PARC—**David Ungar** and **Randall B. Smith**—posed a question that startled even devoted Smalltalk veterans: *what if object-oriented programming didn't need classes at all?*

Think about how people actually grasp new ideas in everyday life. Before you ever read a biology textbook defining the abstract category 'Dog,' you met one real, concrete dog—and understood every other dog by comparing it to that familiar example! In class-based languages like Simula, Objective-C, and Eiffel, however, you could never create even a single quirky button without first designing an abstract class blueprint; customizing one unusual object often meant inventing an awkward one-off subclass.

Moving first to **Stanford University** and later to **Sun Microsystems Laboratories (Sun Labs)**, Ungar and Smith created **Self**, a radically minimalist language designed around concrete examples instead of abstract blueprints.

questions.prompt: What everyday observation motivated David Ungar and Randall Smith to question class-based blueprints in Self?
choices: People find abstract taxonomy blueprints far easier to memorize before meeting any concrete example.
Class-based languages prevented programmers from organizing data and actions inside the same object.
People naturally understand categories through concrete examples first rather than abstract blueprints.
Statically typed compilers forbade creating more than one unique button inside a graphical toolkit.
questions.explanation: Ungar and Smith noticed that humans grasp concepts through concrete exemplars first, whereas class-based languages forced programmers to invent abstract blueprints before making even one object.

questions.prompt: At which research institutions was Self primarily developed after Ungar and Smith sparked the idea at Xerox PARC?
choices: Stanford University and Sun Microsystems Laboratories.
CERN in Switzerland and Stepstone in Connecticut.
Interactive Software Engineering and Apple in Cupertino.
The Norwegian Computing Center and Bell Laboratories.
questions.explanation: Conceived at Xerox PARC in 1986–1987, Self was built and refined primarily at Stanford University and then Sun Microsystems Laboratories (Sun Labs).

chunks.title: Prototype-Based Inheritance and Cloning
chunks.content_markdown:
Self discarded classes entirely in favor of **prototype-based inheritance**: an object model made exclusively of concrete, live exemplar objects called **prototypes**. Instead of stamping new objects from an abstract class blueprint, you create a new object by **cloning**—directly duplicating an existing concrete prototype and tweaking whichever details you want to differ.

Picture needing a new customer invoice in a busy office. Rather than drafting a formal typesetting template from scratch, you grab a filled-out sample invoice sitting on your desk, run it through the photocopier, and pencil in the new buyer's name and amount! And how do cloned objects share common behavior without classes? Every object can point to another live prototype—typically a shared 'traits' object holding reusable methods. When an object receives a message it doesn't recognize locally, it simply forwards the lookup up to its parent prototype.

questions.prompt: How do programmers create a new object in Self's classless model?
choices: By drafting an abstract class blueprint with explicit inheritance clauses before creating objects.
By defining a compiled C template and routing its creation through 'objc_msgSend'.
By writing executable 'require' and 'ensure' contracts that generate objects at runtime.
By cloning an existing concrete prototype object and adjusting only the differing details.
questions.explanation: Without classes, Self creates new objects via cloning—copying a live exemplar (prototype) directly and modifying only what changes.

questions.prompt: In prototype-based inheritance, how do many cloned objects share common methods without belonging to a class?
choices: The runtime stores every method inside one global C function shared by all prototypes.
Each object delegates unanswered messages to a shared parent prototype holding the common behavior.
The compiler copies every method's full code separately into each individual cloned object.
Objects send unanswered messages directly to 'nil' and receive a shared default response.
questions.explanation: Prototype-based inheritance shares behavior by linking objects to a shared parent prototype (such as a traits object) that handles delegated messages.

chunks.title: Uniform Slots: Erasing the Wall Between Data and Methods
chunks.content_markdown:
Self pushed minimalism one astonishing step further by dissolving the wall between stored data fields and executable methods. Inside Self, every object is simply a neat bundle of named compartments called **uniform slots**. Whether a slot holds a stored number, an updater action, a runnable method, or a link to a parent prototype, outside code interacts with every slot the exact same way—by sending a message!

Walk through a concrete `point` object representing a dot on screen. It holds a data slot `x` containing `3`, a data slot `y` containing `4`, assignment slots `x:` and `y:` to update them, and a parent slot (`parent*`) pointing to a shared `pointTraits` prototype containing a method slot `distanceFromOrigin`. Sending `myPoint x` retrieves `3`; sending `myPoint distanceFromOrigin` delegates through `parent*` and computes the distance. Swapping a stored slot for a computed method slot never breaks a single caller.

questions.prompt: What does Self unify inside a single building block called a 'uniform slot'?
choices: Compiled C helper functions, selector tables, and archived Interface Builder canvas layouts.
Static preconditions, postconditions, class invariants, and diamond-inheritance resolution rules.
Stored data values, executable methods, and parent delegation links accessed uniformly via messages.
Abstract class blueprints, static type checks, and automatic reference-counting ownership tallies.
questions.explanation: In Self, stored state, runnable methods, and parent links are all uniform slots accessed identically through message sends.

questions.prompt: Why does Self's uniform-slot design echo Eiffel's uniform access principle while taking it even further?
choices: Callers use identical message syntax for stored or computed slots, letting even one live object swap between them.
Callers use distinct brackets for fields versus methods so the compiler can verify slot layouts beforehand.
Self attaches Eiffel 'require' and 'ensure' contracts to every slot lookup before reading any stored value.
Self eliminates message passing on stored numbers so coordinate reads compile directly via static dispatch.
questions.explanation: Just as Eiffel hid stored fields versus computed queries behind one notation, Self makes every slot access a message—letting even a single live object replace stored data with computed behavior seamlessly.

chunks.title: Dynamic Parent Swapping and the Tactile Morphic World
chunks.content_markdown:
Because parent links in Self were simply ordinary slots marked with a trailing star (`parent*`), inheritance itself was no longer frozen at compile time—a living object could actually **reassign its parent slot while the program ran**!

Imagine a graphical window object whose parent slot points to `expandedWindowTraits` when open, and switches to `minimizedIconTraits` when collapsed. With one single slot assignment, the window transforms its entire set of behaviors cleanly—no tangled `if minimized` checks scattered through dozens of methods. Even Self's pioneering graphical workspace, **Morphic** (developed at Sun Labs and later adopted by Squeak Smalltalk), brought this concrete spirit straight to the screen. Buttons, clocks, and drawings behaved like physical objects you could pick up with the mouse, peel open to inspect their slots, duplicate with a click, and wire together live while watching them run.

questions.prompt: What unusual runtime capability followed directly from making parent links ordinary slots in Self?
choices: Objects became permanently immutable after cloning so no stored data could ever change.
An object could switch its parent prototype at runtime to transform its entire behavior set.
The compiler could determine every object's exact memory layout before the program launched.
Every prototype automatically inherited from two diamond-shaped parent objects at the same time.
questions.explanation: Because parent references are mutable slots, a live Self object can swap its parent prototype at runtime—dynamically changing which behaviors it inherits.

questions.prompt: How did Self's 'Morphic' user interface reflect the philosophy of prototype-based programming?
choices: It displayed static text-only class hierarchies that programmers had to edit before compiling.
It locked graphical widgets inside pre-compiled libraries whose internals stayed hidden at runtime.
It required drafting abstract layout templates before creating a single button on screen.
It let users directly grab, inspect, clone, and rewire live graphical objects on screen.
questions.explanation: Morphic embodied Self's concrete, exemplar-first worldview by letting people directly manipulate, inspect, and clone live visual objects on the screen.

chunks.title: Index-Card Simplicity Meets a Looming Speed Crisis
chunks.content_markdown:
Self achieved a breathtaking feat of conceptual economy: no classes, no separate syntax for variables versus methods, no rigid inheritance trees—just concrete prototypes, cloning, uniform slots, and delegating parents. You could explain Self's entire core design on a single index card! That elegance left a lasting imprint on language history: in 1995, Netscape's Brendan Eich drew directly on Self's prototype-based inheritance when creating **JavaScript** for the emerging World Wide Web.

Yet in the late 1980s, Self's radical purity carried a daunting engineering question. Objective-C got its speed by dropping down to direct compiled C; Eiffel got its speed by locking down static class layouts before execution. Self threw away *both* C shortcuts *and* static classes—turning even the tiniest field read or math step into a dynamic message send! Next, we examine why pure classless messaging initially ran painfully slowly—and why critics bet it could never be fixed.

questions.prompt: Which hugely influential 1995 Web programming language borrowed Self's prototype-based inheritance model directly?
choices: JavaScript, created by Brendan Eich at Netscape.
Eiffel, created by Bertrand Meyer in Paris.
Objective-C, created by Brad Cox and Tom Love.
Simula 67, created at the Norwegian Computing Center.
questions.explanation: Brendan Eich directly adopted Self's classless, prototype-based inheritance model when designing JavaScript in 1995.

questions.prompt: Why did Self's design pose an even harder performance challenge than Objective-C or Eiffel?
choices: Self prohibited cloning more than one numeric prototype inside any graphical application.
Self required manual reference counting on every single integer operation inside a loop.
Self dropped both C escape hatches and static layouts, routing every step through messages.
Self forced objects to resolve diamond inheritance conflicts manually before reading any slot.
questions.explanation: Without C's bare-metal layer or static class layouts, pure Self relied on dynamic slot lookup for every tiny operation, creating a massive raw-speed challenge.

sections.title: 8. The Purity Tax: Why Pure Classless Message Passing Ran Painfully Slow
sections.summary: Explains the daunting runtime bottleneck behind Self's elegance: without static classes, fixed memory layouts, or built-in primitive shortcuts, even basic arithmetic, loop steps, conditionals, and field reads become dynamically dispatched messages. Walks through how repeated lookup-chain walks and per-clone slot metadata initially made pure classless programs run tens to hundreds of times slower than C—seemingly confirming late-1980s skepticism that pure dynamic OOP could never achieve native speed.

chunks.title: A Language Too Pure for 1980s Silicon
chunks.content_markdown:
On a whiteboard, Self looked like perfection: one tiny, unified rule—send a message to a prototype—replaced classes, fields, methods, and control structures all at once. On late-1980s workstation silicon, however, Self's earliest experimental implementations hit a brutal wall: straightforward programs ran **tens to hundreds of times slower than compiled C**!

Imagine unveiling an exquisitely minimalist racing bicycle only to realize it crawls slower than walking. Skeptics of dynamic object orientation felt completely vindicated. Even Smalltalk—which still kept classes and built-in shortcuts for reading an object's private variables—had struggled to match compiled speed on 1980s desktops. Stripping away classes *and* turning every simple variable read into a full dynamic message looked like computational fantasy. To appreciate the astonishing virtual-machine breakthrough that rescued Self, we first have to see *why* pure classless messaging imposed such a punishing 'purity tax.'

questions.prompt: How did early naive implementations of Self compare in raw execution speed to compiled C on late-1980s hardware?
choices: They matched compiled C right away because removing classes eliminated unnecessary blueprint checks.
They outran C on tight numeric loops while lagging slightly during graphical refreshes.
They ran only about ten percent slower than C thanks to built-in variable shortcuts.
They ran tens to hundreds of times slower than C, reinforcing skepticism of dynamic OOP.
questions.explanation: Early unoptimized Self runtimes ran tens to hundreds of times slower than C, leading many skeptics to assume pure classless message passing could never be fast.

questions.prompt: Why did Self look even harder to make fast than 1980s Smalltalk?
choices: Smalltalk compiled every program into static C functions ahead of time without a virtual machine.
Self dropped even Smalltalk's classes and private-variable shortcuts, making every read a dynamic message.
Smalltalk banned objects from inheriting behavior, whereas Self required deep diamond class hierarchies.
Self lacked a virtual machine entirely and interpreted every prototype directly from text source files.
questions.explanation: Smalltalk still had fixed classes and direct access to instance variables inside methods; Self removed both, turning even basic field reads into dynamic message sends.

chunks.title: The Anatomy of Dispatch Overhead
chunks.content_markdown:
To understand Self's bottleneck, compare how a **CPU** (central processing unit, the computer's main processor chip) prefers to work against what pure message passing demands. A CPU thrives on fixed, predictable shortcuts: if a static compiler knows `point.x` always sits eight **bytes** (tiny standard units of memory) past the start of every `Point`, reading `x` takes one crisp memory instruction lasting a few nanoseconds.

Without static classes, the virtual machine cannot assume where `x` lives—or even whether `x` is stored data or a computed method! Every step therefore pays **dispatch overhead**: the extra CPU cycles and memory fetches spent *finding* which slot or method to run rather than doing the useful work itself.

Picture a chef cooking soup who walks to the back office to check a filing cabinet for where the salt shaker lives today, walks back, sprinkles one pinch, and repeats the entire office trip for the very next pinch!

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is 'dispatch overhead' inside a dynamic object-oriented runtime?
choices: The extra CPU time spent locating which slot or method to run rather than doing the core work.
The startup pause caused when a static compiler checks every class blueprint before launching a program.
The extra memory consumed when programmers manually retain objects inside a circular reference cycle.
The time spent translating human-readable English keywords into fixed byte offsets ahead of execution.
questions.explanation: Dispatch overhead is the extra runtime cost of searching for the right target slot or method instead of executing the actual underlying computation.

questions.prompt: Why can a compiled static language read 'point.x' with almost zero dispatch overhead compared to pure Self?
choices: Static languages store every number inside one shared global variable without creating separate objects.
Static languages cache recently used coordinate values automatically inside a runtime method notepad.
Static compilers know every class's fixed byte layout beforehand and compile 'point.x' to one direct load.
Static languages skip reading stored coordinates from memory whenever a loop executes repeatedly.
questions.explanation: Because static classes lock down fixed memory layouts before execution, reading a field compiles straight into a direct byte-offset load without any runtime lookup.

chunks.title: Walkthrough: Counting to a Million Through Lookup Chains
chunks.content_markdown:
Trace something utterly mundane—a simple loop summing the integers from one to a million by checking `i < limit` and updating `sum` with `sum + i`.

In compiled C, that entire loop body shrinks to three or four raw machine instructions spinning right inside the processor's fastest on-chip storage. Now trace pure, unoptimized Self! Even reading `i` sends a message to the running method's local object. Testing `i < limit` sends `<` to an integer object, forcing the virtual machine to walk its **lookup chain**—the sequence of parent-slot hops from an object up through its parent prototypes until it finds a matching slot. Branching on the result sends an `ifTrue:` message to a boolean object (`true` or `false`). Computing `sum + i` triggers another lookup chain for `+`, and storing the result sends `sum:`!

One tiny loop step that took three instructions in C explodes into dozens of dynamic lookups—repeated a million times!

questions.prompt: What is a 'lookup chain' in a prototype-based runtime like Self?
choices: A compile-time checklist that converts Eiffel preconditions directly into native processor instructions.
The sequence of parent-slot hops a runtime traverses upward from an object to locate a slot.
A circular ownership loop between two objects that keeps their reference counts above zero.
A printed directory of fixed memory addresses wired before a compiled program launches.
questions.explanation: When an object does not define a requested slot locally, the VM follows its parent slots step by step—walking the lookup chain—until it finds the matching slot.

questions.prompt: Why does a simple counting loop run dramatically slower in naive Self than in compiled C?
choices: Self forbids integer prototypes from storing numbers above one thousand inside main memory.
Compiled C skips checking loop conditions after the first pass, whereas Self checks every iteration.
Self runs automatic garbage collection after every single addition step inside a numeric loop.
Even tiny steps like reading variables, comparing numbers, branching, and adding trigger dynamic lookups.
questions.explanation: Because pure Self turns every micro-operation—variable access, comparisons, boolean branches, arithmetic, and updates—into dynamic message sends, dispatch overhead multiplies across every single loop tick.

chunks.title: The Hidden Memory Explosion of Naive Cloning
chunks.content_markdown:
Slow lookup chains were only half of the purity tax—naive classless cloning also triggered a stealthy **memory explosion**.

Suppose a scientific visualization clones a `point` prototype one hundred thousand times to plot a dense star map. In a class-based language like Simula or Eiffel, the `Point` class stores the **metadata** (descriptive bookkeeping information such as field names `x` and `y` and shared method links) *just once* in one central blueprint. Each individual point object therefore needs only a tiny handful of bytes for its two coordinate numbers.

In a naive classless virtual machine, however, every cloned object is an independent container carrying its own full copy of slot names, descriptors, and parent pointers! Clone `point` one hundred thousand times and you store identical metadata one hundred thousand separate times. That bloated footprint overflows the CPU's fast local caches and clogs memory traffic—piling a severe memory penalty right onto dispatch overhead.

questions.prompt: Why did naive prototype cloning consume far more memory than class-based creation when making 100,000 'point' objects?
choices: Prototype objects stored each numeric coordinate as long uncompressed text strings instead of compact numbers.
Class-based languages automatically merged identical coordinates into a single shared point in main memory.
Each cloned object naively duplicated its own slot names and metadata instead of sharing one blueprint.
Prototype-based virtual machines kept every older version of a cloned object archived permanently in memory.
questions.explanation: Without a shared blueprint, naively giving every clone its own copy of slot names and metadata repeats identical structural information across every single instance.

questions.prompt: Beyond wasting main memory, how did bloated per-object metadata worsen execution speed in early Self?
choices: Oversized objects overflowed fast CPU caches and increased memory traffic, compounding dispatch overhead.
Oversized objects automatically disabled dynamic dispatch and severed parent delegation chains.
Oversized objects forced the virtual machine to fall back to manual reference counting on clones.
Oversized objects stopped integer prototypes from answering arithmetic messages inside tight loops.
questions.explanation: When objects swell with duplicated metadata, fewer fit inside fast processor caches, forcing slower trips to main memory on top of repeated slot lookups.

chunks.title: Refusing to Compromise: The Challenge That Reinvented VMs
chunks.content_markdown:
By 1988, Self stood at a make-or-break crossroads. Stripping away classes, static types, and primitive shortcuts had exposed the full cost of purity: heavy dispatch overhead on every tiny operation, endless lookup-chain hops, and bloated per-clone memory layouts.

Conventional computer-science wisdom insisted only two doors were open. Either compromise the language—bolting static type annotations or C escape hatches back onto Self—or accept defeat and leave Self as a slow classroom curiosity forever. David Ungar and two brilliant Stanford doctoral students, **Craig Chambers** and **Urs Hölzle**, rejected both doors!

They asked a radically different question: *even though Self ALLOWS any object to morph wildly at runtime, how do real programs actually behave in practice?* Most clones of `point` keep the exact same slots, and most message sites see the same one or two object shapes over and over! Turning that observation into working virtual-machine machinery is our next chapter.

questions.prompt: How did David Ungar, Craig Chambers, and Urs Hölzle choose to confront Self's steep speed bottleneck?
choices: They added mandatory C syntax and static types so programmers bypassed dynamic messaging manually.
They abandoned prototype inheritance and rebuilt their graphical workspace atop Simula's static classes.
They accepted slow execution permanently and positioned Self strictly as an introductory teaching tool.
They kept the pure classless language intact and engineered a far smarter virtual machine.
questions.explanation: Rather than compromising Self's minimalist design, Ungar, Chambers, and Hölzle kept the language pure and invented revolutionary VM optimizations.

questions.prompt: What key empirical observation about real dynamic programs unlocked the Self team's virtual-machine breakthroughs?
choices: Real programs rarely clone the same prototype more than a few times during an entire session.
Clones typically share identical slot layouts, and call sites repeatedly see the same few shapes.
Dynamic programs spend nearly all their runtime managing circular retain cycles rather than sending messages.
Real programs alter every object's parent slot continuously, preventing any shape from repeating twice.
questions.explanation: Real programs exhibit massive regularity at runtime: clones from the same prototype almost always share identical layouts, and individual call sites typically see only one or a few shapes.

sections.title: 9. Reinventing the VM: Object Maps, PICs & Runtime Type Feedback
sections.summary: Follows Stanford researchers Craig Chambers and Urs Hölzle as they overturned conventional wisdom by exploiting how real dynamic programs actually behave. Unpacks three interlocking VM inventions from first principles: internal object 'maps' (later known as hidden classes) factoring shared slot layouts out of individual clones, polymorphic inline caches (PICs) remembering multiple observed maps directly at each call site, and runtime type feedback harvesting live PIC observations to guide optimization without programmer type annotations.

chunks.title: Finding Hidden Regularity Inside Dynamic Freedom
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch weekday morning traffic from a helicopter. Legally, every driver *could* take a wildly different detour through back alleys every morning—yet in reality, ninety-nine percent of commuters cruise down the exact same highway lane day after day!

At Stanford between 1989 and 1994, **Craig Chambers** and **Urs Hölzle** discovered the exact same hidden order inside running Self programs. Even though Self contained *no classes* in its source language and permitted any prototype to add or delete slots on a whim, real programs overwhelmingly cloned thousands of objects sharing identical slot layouts, and individual message call sites repeatedly encountered just one or a few object shapes.

That single realization flipped virtual-machine design upside down. If the virtual machine could quietly notice and exploit those recurring shapes *while the program ran*, it could win back the compactness and speed of static classes without ever forcing classes back onto the programmer.

questions.prompt: What hidden runtime pattern did Craig Chambers and Urs Hölzle observe inside real Self programs?
choices: Despite dynamic freedom, clones kept identical slot shapes and call sites repeatedly saw the same few shapes.
Nearly every cloned object renamed its slots continuously so no two clones ever shared a layout.
Self programmers quietly inserted compiled C headers whenever loops needed to avoid dynamic message lookups.
Real Self programs rarely cloned prototypes more than three times inside any single running session.
questions.explanation: Even though Self allowed arbitrary runtime mutation, real programs behaved with strong regularity—clones shared shapes and call sites saw only a small set of shapes.

questions.prompt: Why was the commuter-traffic insight so transformative for virtual-machine design?
choices: It proved dynamic languages could achieve speed only by forbidding runtime edits to prototype slots.
It showed programmers had to add explicit Eiffel preconditions so virtual machines could predict shapes.
It showed the VM itself could detect recurring shapes at runtime to recover static-like efficiency.
It convinced researchers to discard virtual machines and run prototypes strictly via static compilation.
questions.explanation: By discovering structural regularity automatically at runtime, the VM could optimize memory layout and dispatch without compromising Self's classless source model.

chunks.title: Internal Object Maps: Secret Hidden Classes Behind the Curtain
chunks.content_markdown:
Craig Chambers's first breakthrough cured both memory bloat and slow field checks at once: the internal **object map**—an invention later popularized by Google's V8 JavaScript engine under the name **hidden class**.

Imagine printing ten thousand concert tickets for one arena. Nobody prints the entire arena seating chart on every individual ticket stub! Instead, the box office keeps *one* master seating chart and prints just a tiny chart ID plus the buyer's unique row and seat on each stub. Likewise, when a Self program clones a `point` prototype ten thousand times, the VM factors all shared layout metadata—slot names (`x`, `y`), fixed byte offsets, constant parent pointers, and methods—into *one* shared **object map**.

Each individual `point` clone shrinks to a tiny pointer to that map plus its raw values (`3`, `4`). Memory bloat vanishes, fixed offsets return behind the scenes, and checking an object's complete shape takes a single fast pointer comparison!

questions.prompt: How does an internal 'object map' solve the memory explosion of cloning 10,000 identical 'point' prototypes?
choices: It deletes unused coordinate values from main memory until a drawing loop requests those specific points.
It compresses every point's slot names and coordinates into a single shared text archive on disk.
It forces all ten thousand cloned points to point to the exact same shared coordinate numbers.
It stores shared slot names and offsets once in a map while each clone keeps a pointer and data.
questions.explanation: Factoring identical structural metadata into one shared object map lets every clone store just a pointer to the map plus its individual data values.

questions.prompt: Besides shrinking memory usage, what major speed benefit does giving clones a shared object map unlock?
choices: It lets the runtime skip garbage collection permanently on every cloned object sharing that map.
It lets the VM confirm an object's entire shape in one pointer check and read fixed offsets.
It lets the compiler enforce static Eiffel type annotations across every prototype before startup.
It removes all parent delegation links so every clone holds its own private method copies.
questions.explanation: Because a map encodes exact slot names and byte offsets, matching one pointer confirms an object's entire shape and lets the VM read fields at known offsets.

chunks.title: Walkthrough: Polymorphic Inline Caches (PICs) at Work
chunks.content_markdown:
With object maps in place, Urs Hölzle attacked dynamic dispatch overhead right at each **call site**—the specific line of code sending a message like `shape draw`. Earlier 1980s Smalltalk VMs (pioneered by L. Peter Deutsch and Allan Schiffman) used a **monomorphic inline cache**: remembering the *single* most recently seen class right at that call site. That flew when only circles arrived—but thrashed constantly on a mixed list of `Circle`, `Rectangle`, and `Triangle`, wiping and refilling its lone entry on every turn!

In 1991, Hölzle invented the **polymorphic inline cache (PIC)**: a tiny, dynamically generated shortcut snippet (a **stub**) attached to the call site that remembers a *small list* of recently seen object maps. Step through `shape draw` as mixed shapes stream past: the PIC checks 'Circle map? Jump to `Circle.draw`! Rectangle map? Jump to `Rectangle.draw`! Triangle map? Jump to `Triangle.draw`!' Only a brand-new map falls back to the slow lookup chain.

questions.prompt: What limitation of earlier monomorphic (single-type) inline caches did Urs Hölzle's polymorphic inline cache (PIC) overcome?
choices: Single-type caches thrashed when call sites saw multiple alternating shapes, whereas a PIC caches several maps.
Single-type caches worked only for static C functions, whereas a PIC worked strictly inside classless prototypes.
Single-type caches froze an object's numeric fields permanently, whereas a PIC let values update at runtime.
Single-type caches required programmers to declare every shape upfront, whereas a PIC eliminated object maps.
questions.explanation: A monomorphic cache stores only one recently seen type and constantly misses on mixed collections, while a PIC checks a small list of observed maps directly at the call site.

questions.prompt: In the 'shape draw' walkthrough, when does the virtual machine still need to fall back to walking the full lookup chain?
choices: Every time 'shape draw' switches back and forth between two already-cached shape maps.
Whenever the PIC shortcut snippet matches an incoming shape's map on the first check.
Every time the drawing loop reads a stored data slot instead of calling a method.
Only when an incoming shape carries an object map the PIC has not yet recorded.
questions.explanation: Known maps cached inside the PIC jump directly to their matching methods; only an unseen map falls back to a full lookup-chain search (and can then be added to the PIC).

chunks.title: The Surprise Bonus: PICs as Live Spies for Type Feedback
chunks.content_markdown:
Polymorphic inline caches sped up mixed call sites dramatically—yet Urs Hölzle spotted an even deeper treasure sitting right inside them. Look at what a PIC quietly builds as a program runs: right at `shape draw`, the PIC holds a live, ground-truth record of *exactly which concrete object maps actually arrived at that line of code!*

Hölzle called this breakthrough **type feedback**: inspecting the maps recorded inside live inline caches so the virtual machine learns the real types flowing through every corner of a program—without the programmer ever typing a single static type declaration! Even better, maps stayed completely faithful to Self's live dynamism. If one quirky `point` suddenly adds a brand-new `z` slot at runtime, the VM simply transitions that *single* object onto a fresh three-slot map while leaving the other 99,999 ordinary points untouched on their shared two-slot map. Zero freedom lost!

questions.prompt: What is 'type feedback' in Self's virtual machine architecture?
choices: Automated compiler warnings alerting programmers when a prototype omits an expected numeric slot.
A static checklist requiring developers to annotate every call site with strict Eiffel types.
Reading live receiver maps recorded inside inline caches to learn which shapes actually reach each call site.
A visual inspector that notifies users whenever a prototype switches its parent link on screen.
questions.explanation: Type feedback reuses the exact receiver maps already collected by inline caches during execution, giving the VM concrete runtime type profiles automatically.

questions.prompt: How does Self's object-map system preserve full dynamic flexibility if a single clone adds a brand-new slot at runtime?
choices: It halts execution with a type error forbidding any clone from adding new slots.
It moves that one modified object to a new map without disturbing unmodified clones.
It forces every other clone sharing the old map to add the same new slot.
It disables polymorphic inline caches across the entire program for the rest of execution.
questions.explanation: When one clone's structure changes, only that object transitions to a new map—preserving both compact sharing for the unchanged clones and full dynamic freedom.

chunks.title: Static-Quality Knowledge Without Static Chains
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and appreciate the three-part engine Chambers and Hölzle had assembled inside Self's virtual machine.

First, internal **object maps** secretly restored the compact memory footprints and fixed byte offsets of static classes behind the scenes while leaving the language completely classless on the surface. Second, **polymorphic inline caches** eliminated repeated lookup-chain walks even at mixed-type call sites. Third, **type feedback** turned those caches into free runtime spies, handing the VM accurate knowledge of real receiver shapes that rivaled—and sometimes outperformed—static type annotations!

Yet jumping out to a PIC stub on every tiny `+` or `x` message still left substantial speed on the table compared to hand-tuned C. Armed with rich live type feedback, could the VM stop merely *caching* message calls and instead *erase* them on the fly—compiling hot code into tight native instructions while staying safe if assumptions broke? That crowning leap finishes our journey next.

questions.prompt: How do object maps, polymorphic inline caches, and type feedback work together as a unified pipeline inside Self's VM?
choices: Maps give clones shared shape IDs, PICs cache observed maps per site, and type feedback profiles real types.
Maps enforce class invariants, PICs manage reference counts, and type feedback compiles prototypes into static C files.
Maps replace parent delegation with diamond hierarchies, PICs merge duplicate slots, and type feedback disables dynamic cloning.
Maps compress disk images, PICs check preconditions ahead of time, and type feedback blocks new shapes from loading.
questions.explanation: Each mechanism feeds the next: maps identify object shapes compactly, PICs record observed maps at each call site for fast routing, and type feedback turns those PIC records into live optimization profiles.

questions.prompt: Even with object maps and PICs working smoothly, why did pure Self still trail optimized C on tight numeric loops?
choices: Object maps prevented integer prototypes from using fixed byte offsets during basic arithmetic.
Polymorphic inline caches worked only for graphical drawing messages and ignored numeric slots.
Type feedback paused every numeric loop periodically to rewrite all shared object maps.
Jumping through separate call-site stubs on tiny operations still left call boundaries unfused.
questions.explanation: PICs sped up message routing, yet tiny operations still paid call-stub and method-boundary costs until an optimizing compiler could fuse hot calls directly inline.

sections.title: 10. Adaptive JIT, Speculative Inlining, Deoptimization & the Modern VM Legacy
sections.summary: Completes Self's VM revolution by tracing how adaptive JIT compilation focuses optimization on 'hot' execution paths, how speculative inlining uses type feedback to fold likely target methods directly into callers behind lightweight map checks for near-C speed, and how dynamic deoptimization safely bails out to unoptimized frames whenever assumptions break or code changes live. Concludes with Self's historic paradox: fading as a daily language while donating prototypes to JavaScript and handing its adaptive VM architecture directly to Java's HotSpot JVM, Google's V8, and every modern dynamic runtime.

chunks.title: Don't Polish Cold Code: Finding the Hot Paths
chunks.content_markdown:
By 1993, Self's virtual machine had a gold mine of live type feedback sitting inside its polymorphic inline caches. Yet unleashing a heavy, perfectionist compiler on *every* method before a program started caused a miserable new problem: sluggish launch pauses! Nobody wanted to wait ten seconds for an editor to open while the VM painstakingly polished thousands of initialization routines that would execute only *once* and never run again.

In his landmark 1994 Stanford PhD dissertation, **Urs Hölzle** leaned on an enduring law of real software: programs typically spend roughly ninety percent of their time executing less than ten percent of their code—the **hot paths**, such as inner calculation loops and frequent screen redraws. Instead of compiling everything aggressively upfront, Self started almost instantaneously using a lightweight, fast baseline compiler, tracked simple invocation counters to detect which methods ran hottest, and invested heavy optimization strictly where it actually mattered.

questions.prompt: Why did eagerly running a heavy optimizing compiler on every method at startup hurt interactive Self programs?
choices: Heavy compilers lacked access to object maps and therefore refused to optimize cloned prototypes.
Optimizing startup routines wiped out polymorphic inline caches before inner loops could fill them.
It wasted launch time polishing cold one-time setup code instead of focusing on repeated paths.
Heavy compilation consumed all main memory, forcing the VM to disable automatic garbage collection.
questions.explanation: Most code runs rarely or only once during startup; investing heavy compilation time uniformly caused noticeable pauses with almost zero payoff on cold code.

questions.prompt: What runtime signal did Self's VM monitor to decide which methods deserved aggressive optimization?
choices: Invocation and loop counters pinpointing the small fraction of 'hot' paths consuming most time.
Static priority tags inserted manually by programmers beside every speed-critical prototype method.
Object-map sizes indicating which prototypes stored the largest number of separate data slots.
Parent-chain lengths showing which inherited methods sat farthest away from their calling objects.
questions.explanation: Tracking simple execution counters revealed the hot paths—typically a tiny fraction of the program responsible for the vast majority of CPU time.

chunks.title: Adaptive JIT Compilation and Speculative Inlining
chunks.content_markdown:
Targeting optimization toward hot paths while a program runs is called **adaptive JIT compilation** ('Just-In-Time' compilation)—translating hot code into tight native machine instructions on the fly using live execution profiles.

Its sharpest weapon was **speculative inlining**. Normally, calling a method jumps away to a separate routine; **inlining** instead pastes the target method's instructions straight into the caller so the call boundary vanishes completely! A static compiler can inline only when it is one hundred percent sure of the target ahead of time. Armed with live type feedback, Self's adaptive JIT took smart, calculated bets: 'At this hot loop, every receiver so far carried the `Point` map—so paste `Point`'s coordinate load directly here behind a tiny one-instruction map check!'

Suddenly, dynamic message boundaries inside hot loops evaporated, letting standard native optimizations collapse arithmetic and field reads into raw hardware instructions—propelling pure, classless Self to roughly half the speed of hand-tuned C!

questions.prompt: What makes 'speculative inlining' different from traditional static inlining in a language like C?
choices: Speculative inlining removes runtime map checks entirely so every incoming object runs identical instructions.
Speculative inlining bets on live type feedback and pastes target code behind fast runtime guards.
Speculative inlining compiles every method ahead of launch without waiting for runtime execution profiles.
Speculative inlining copies target methods only for static classes and skips dynamic prototype slots.
questions.explanation: Unlike static inlining, which requires compile-time certainty, speculative inlining bets on runtime type feedback and inserts a fast map check before the pasted target code.

questions.prompt: How did speculative inlining transform the execution speed of pure, classless Self programs?
choices: It slowed hot loops slightly to pay for map guards while accelerating cold startup code.
It matched C's speed strictly by replacing garbage collection with manual reference counting.
It accelerated graphical rendering alone while leaving numeric arithmetic bound to full lookup chains.
It erased dynamic call boundaries in hot loops, bringing Self near half of C's speed.
questions.explanation: By erasing tiny message-call boundaries behind lightweight map guards, speculative inlining exposed hot loops to classic native optimizations, closing nearly all of the speed gap to C.

chunks.title: Walkthrough: The Safety Parachute of Dynamic Deoptimization
chunks.content_markdown:
One nail-biting question remained: *what happens when a speculative bet turns out wrong?* Imagine our hot counting loop was speculatively inlined assuming `sum + i` always receives `Integer` objects—and twenty minutes later, an exotic `Fraction` object arrives, or a programmer pauses execution and edits a method live in the debugger! Without a safety net, that tightly fused native machine code would crash or produce wrong answers.

Hölzle, Chambers, and Ungar solved this with **dynamic deoptimization**—a mid-flight safety parachute. Trace what happens step by step when that tiny one-instruction map check fails: the VM halts the optimized shortcut, consults saved compiler translation notes, cleanly unpacks the single fused native **stack frame** (the live workspace holding an active routine's temporary values) back into ordinary, unoptimized virtual-machine frames, and resumes right at the exact interrupted step! Users got native-level speed on the hot path *and* rock-solid dynamic semantics and live debugging whenever reality changed.

questions.prompt: What triggers 'dynamic deoptimization' inside an adaptive JIT virtual machine?
choices: A hot method finishing its loop without ever encountering an unexpected receiver map.
A programmer marking a routine with explicit static type annotations before startup.
A failed speculative guard from an unexpected object map or a live debugging edit.
An automatic garbage-collection sweep freeing abandoned clones inside an idle background window.
questions.explanation: Whenever an optimistic assumption breaks at a map guard (or live code/debugging changes require unoptimized frames), the VM triggers dynamic deoptimization.

questions.prompt: During dynamic deoptimization, how does the VM safely recover without crashing or losing the program's current work?
choices: It restarts the entire hot loop from its first iteration using the unoptimized baseline compiler.
It unpacks the optimized stack frame into unoptimized VM frames via saved notes and resumes.
It silently ignores the unexpected object map and returns zero to keep the loop running.
It freezes the running method until the programmer recompiles the source file into plain C.
questions.explanation: Using saved compiler translation notes, dynamic deoptimization converts the fused optimized stack frame back into clean unoptimized VM frames right at the exact execution point.

chunks.title: The Language That Faded—and Quietly Conquered the World
chunks.content_markdown:
Technology history rarely delivers a richer paradox than Self's aftermath. As a daily programming language, **Self** faded quietly during the late 1990s: its workstation niche and unfamiliar classless style never won mainstream corporate adoption. Yet Self's inventions conquered modern computing along *two* unstoppable highways!

On the language highway, Self donated prototype-based inheritance straight to **JavaScript** (1995), soon running inside every Web browser on the planet. On the virtual-machine highway, Self's VM pioneers—including **Urs Hölzle** and Danish VM architect **Lars Bak**—carried adaptive JIT compilation, type feedback, speculative inlining, and dynamic deoptimization to a startup called **Animorphic Systems**, which Sun Microsystems acquired in 1997 to build Java's flagship **HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM)** (1999). Years later, Lars Bak led Google's **V8** JavaScript engine (2008), putting Self's exact object maps (hidden classes), inline caches, and speculative JIT beneath the modern interactive Web!

questions.prompt: Which two landmark mainstream runtimes directly inherited Self's adaptive VM techniques through pioneers like Urs Hölzle and Lars Bak?
choices: Sun's HotSpot Java Virtual Machine and Google's V8 JavaScript engine.
Stepstone's Objective-C preprocessor and NeXTSTEP's Interface Builder archive loader.
Simula 67's original Oslo compiler and Bertrand Meyer's Eiffel contract runtime.
Xerox PARC's 1972 Smalltalk interpreter and Apple's automatic reference-counting compiler.
questions.explanation: Via Animorphic Systems (acquired by Sun in 1997) and later Google, Self's adaptive VM pioneers built both Java's HotSpot JVM and V8—spreading Self's VM architecture across modern computing.

questions.prompt: What is the great historical paradox of Self's legacy in programming-language history?
choices: Self dominated corporate software for decades, yet none of its VM ideas survived into modern runtimes.
Self proved prototype inheritance could never work outside Stanford's custom workstation graphics environment.
Self achieved C-like speed only by abandoning adaptive VMs in favor of static Eiffel classes.
Self faded as a daily language, yet donated prototypes to JavaScript and adaptive VMs to modern runtimes.
questions.explanation: Although few programmers write Self today, its prototypes live on in JavaScript and its adaptive VM breakthroughs power Java, JavaScript, and virtually every high-speed dynamic runtime.

chunks.title: Synthesizing Three Paths—and Crossing into the Mainstream Era
chunks.content_markdown:
Look back across the remarkable journey from the 1980s crossroads to 2005. Confronted with Simula's static rigidity and Smalltalk's runtime speed gap, three diverging paths stretched object orientation in every direction.

**Objective-C** bridged compiled C with Smalltalk messaging (`objc_msgSend`), powering NeXTSTEP's Interface Builder, dynamic delegation, and categories all the way into Apple's macOS and iOS. **Eiffel** championed European static reliability, clean syntax, built-in garbage collection, and **Design by Contract**—while teaching unforgettable type-system lessons through diamond multiple inheritance and covariant arguments. **Self** stripped away classes for prototypes and uniform slots, triggering a speed crisis that forced Chambers and Hölzle to invent object maps, PICs, type feedback, adaptive JIT compilation, speculative inlining, and dynamic deoptimization.

By proving virtual machines could reconcile dynamic flexibility with near-native speed, Self unlocked the next great chapter: how OOP's two souls collided inside Java, C#, Python, Ruby, and JavaScript in Part 3.

questions.prompt: How did Self's adaptive VM revolution permanently change the original 1980s trade-off that opened this module?
choices: It proved static compilers were obsolete and banished fixed class blueprints from all later languages.
It confirmed industry doubts that dynamic message passing could never rival compiled code speed.
It showed runtime-guided adaptive compilation could pair near-native speed with full dynamic flexibility.
It pushed every later runtime to adopt Objective-C's manual reference counting inside tight loops.
questions.explanation: By combining maps, PICs, type feedback, speculative inlining, and deoptimization, Self broke the old assumption that dynamic dispatch permanently doomed software to slow execution.

questions.prompt: Which pairing accurately matches all three paths of Part 2 to their signature lasting contributions?
choices: Objective-C: executable contracts and covariance; Eiffel: prototype cloning and Morphic; Self: visual Interface Builder categories.
Objective-C: dynamic GUI culture via 'objc_msgSend'; Eiffel: Design by Contract and subtyping lessons; Self: prototypes and adaptive VMs.
Objective-C: polymorphic inline caches and maps; Eiffel: dynamic parent-slot swapping; Self: manual reference counting and ARC.
Objective-C: explicit diamond 'rename' clauses; Eiffel: hidden-class object maps; Self: strict C superset compatibility.
questions.explanation: Objective-C carried Smalltalk's dynamic GUI culture into macOS/iOS; Eiffel gave us Design by Contract and vital multiple-inheritance/variance lessons; Self gave us prototypes and modern adaptive VMs.
